newsitem.title: USA: IBM CEO optimistic about network computers.
newsitem.headline: IBM CEO optimistic about network computers.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp chairman and CEO Louis Gerstner said the computer giant's new network computers are "very compelling" and by 1997, there will be "tens of thousands" of them in use by IBM customers.
But Gerstner told reporters in brief comments at the IBM booth at the Internet World show that he does not see the much- hyped network computers replacing personal computers.
"I think we are going to sell a lot of PCs for a long, long time," Gerstner said.

IBM was the first computer maker to develop and make available a network computer, the low-cost, scaled-down devices that are designed to access corporate networks and the Internet. IBM unveiled its Network Station in September and it is now shipping it in limited quantities.
Volume production will begin early next year.
"Lots of customers will buy NCs, but others will want full function PCs, and others will want TVs with set top boxes," Gerstner said in his keynote address.
Gerstner said that as a multibillion PC maker, IBM is "not agonizing" about the ongoing industry debate over PCs and NCs.
Sun Microsystems Inc, one of the main proponents behind network computers, also recently introduced its JavaStation, its foray into the NC market.

Last month, IBM formed a network computing unit, which is part of its personal systems business, which develops and manufactures personal computers. The NC unit will develop network computers and market them to corporate users.
Gerstner first announced that IBM would develop a network computer at the Comdex trade show in November, 1995, where he also outlined IBM's major focus on networked computing.
